clue.text: Diamonds are a help when dating

definitions.note: a plural example standing for the substance it is made of

blocks.note: first meaning: the element diamonds are made of
second meaning: the radioactive isotope used to date ancient remains

explanation.surface: A cynical tip that a gift of jewellery smooths the path of romance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dating' suggests courtship, but it means fixing the age of old material, as in radiocarbon dating.
explanation.definitionFit: Diamonds are pure crystalline form of this element, and its isotope C-14 lets scientists estimate the age of organic remains.

clue.text: A tribute to Coral Island

blocks.note: taken as written
a toll is a payment exacted, a tribute

explanation.surface: A homage to 'Coral Island', the classic adventure novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals suggest Ballantyne's book 'The Coral Island'; crosswords ignore capitalisation.
explanation.definitionFit: An atoll is a ring-shaped reef of coral enclosing a lagoon.

clue.text: It's no good China entering this game

blocks.note: bad means no good
Minton is a famous make of English porcelain

explanation.surface: A sporting complaint that China joining this contest is unfair.
explanation.walkthrough: China is the porcelain, not the country: Minton is a Staffordshire pottery firm.
explanation.definitionFit: Badminton is the racket sport played with a shuttlecock over a high net.

clue.text: Old lawmaker's modern style

blocks.note: modern means new
ton is fashion or style, from French bon ton

explanation.surface: An ancient legislator's up-to-date fashion sense.
explanation.walkthrough: The lawmaker made scientific laws, not statutes.
explanation.definitionFit: Isaac Newton formulated the laws of motion and gravitation in the seventeenth century.

clue.text: Demanding type making a lot of noise about one

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the noisy word wraps around the single letter

blocks.note: clamant means noisy, clamorous
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A pushy person who makes a racket about a single grievance.
explanation.walkthrough: CLAMANT goes about I to make CLAIMANT.
explanation.definitionFit: A claimant is someone who demands something as their right, such as benefits or compensation.

clue.text: Eccentric provided land and inspiration for sports ground

blocks.note: a card is an eccentric person
if means provided that
a farm is agricultural land
a spark of inspiration

explanation.surface: An odd benefactor donated land and ideas for a stadium.
explanation.walkthrough: Cardiff Arms Park is the famous rugby ground in the Welsh capital.
explanation.definitionFit: Cardiff Arms Park is a stadium in Wales, long the home of Welsh rugby.

clue.text: Africans as hard opponents

blocks.note: taken as written
H is the pencil abbreviation for hard
antis are people opposed to something

explanation.surface: A team of Africans described as tough rivals.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ashanti are a people of Ghana in West Africa, once a powerful kingdom.

clue.text: Music got together, including some biblical text

indicators.note: including means holding something within, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: people who got together met
the Old Testament, part of the Bible

explanation.surface: A choir gathered to set a passage of scripture to music.
explanation.walkthrough: MET holds OT: M-OT-ET.
explanation.definitionFit: A motet is a short unaccompanied choral composition, often on a sacred text.

clue.text: Gain, clearly, from batting practice for match

blocks.note: cricketers practise batting in the nets
pro means in favour of
to fit is to match or suit

explanation.surface: A cricketer gains from net practice before a match.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, nets are the enclosed practice pitches where batsmen train.
explanation.definitionFit: Net profit is the clear gain left after all costs have been deducted.

clue.text: Poet expresses a certain value

blocks.note: to word something is to express it, so 'words' as a verb
worth is the value of something

explanation.surface: A poet's lines are said to convey some definite worth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Expresses' is read as the verb 'words', not as a description of the poet.
explanation.definitionFit: William Wordsworth was the great English Romantic writer of verse, author of 'Daffodils'.

clue.text: Expression of disapproval you heard — such a short skirt!

indicators.note: something heard is only spoken, so the word you is taken by its sound alone

blocks.note: the clicking sound of disapproval
the letter U is pronounced the same as you

explanation.surface: Someone tut-tuts at a scandalously brief skirt.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark keeps the disapproving tone, which supplies the first part.
explanation.definitionFit: A tutu is the very brief, stiff, frilly skirt worn by ballerinas.

clue.text: In England, name one Italian composer

indicators.note: one thing placed in another is enclosed by it

blocks.note: Albion is the old poetic name for England
standard abbreviation for name
Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A request to name a single Italian composer from England.
explanation.walkthrough: N goes inside ALBION to give ALBINON, then I is added: ALBINONI.
explanation.definitionFit: Tomaso Albinoni was a Venetian Baroque musician, famous for the Adagio attributed to him.

clue.text: Kind mother, so-called

blocks.note: first meaning: sort or type, as in 'of that kind'
second meaning: the force personified as Mother

explanation.surface: A gentle maternal figure, so people say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kind' looks like an adjective praising a mother, but it is a noun meaning sort.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means essential character or sort, and the natural world is personified as Mother in the familiar phrase.

clue.text: Light blows returned in petty quarrel

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so the word is read from right to left

blocks.note: taps are gentle blows

explanation.surface: A minor squabble in which gentle slaps are exchanged.
explanation.definitionFit: A spat is a brief, trivial argument or tiff.

clue.text: Sang opera pieces in ecclesiastical residence

indicators.note: broken into pieces, the letters of the preceding words are scattered and reassembled

blocks.note: the fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone sang bits of opera inside a vicar's house.
explanation.definitionFit: A parsonage is the house provided for a parish priest by the church.

clue.text: Peter, after crash, intended to have accident protection

indicators.note: the word given by the clue's first noun is placed behind the other piece

blocks.note: a computer or business crash is a failure
peter is old criminal slang for a safe

explanation.surface: A man called Peter, after a car crash, wishes he'd been insured.
explanation.walkthrough: Peter looks like a name; in underworld slang a peter is a safe, as in peterman, a safecracker.
explanation.definitionFit: A fail-safe device is designed so that when something goes wrong it defaults to a harmless state.

clue.text: The next person hit gold

blocks.note: a hit is a success
or is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: The following competitor struck gold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hit' reads as a verb, but it is a noun: a smash hit.
explanation.definitionFit: A successor is whoever follows another in a role or position.

clue.text: It's a wire fixed up for climber

indicators.note: fixed up means repaired or rearranged, so the letters are put in a new order

blocks.note: the fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: A gardener rigs a wire for a climbing plant to grow up.
explanation.definitionFit: Wisteria is a woody vine that climbs walls with hanging lilac flowers.

clue.text: Where countries meet for complex interchange

indicators.note: complex means intricately tangled, so the letters are mixed up

blocks.note: taken as written
read as inter + change: the word inter, with change a second signal to rearrange it

explanation.surface: A border crossing is a place of complicated exchange.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Interchange' splits: its first part is fodder, its last part the second anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A frontier is the border line between two nations, where their territories touch.

clue.text: Musical tom-tom?

definitions.note: two toms, so a plural noun

blocks.note: first meaning: the Lloyd Webber stage show
second meaning: a tom is a male cat, so tom-tom reads as two of them

explanation.walkthrough: A tom-tom is a drum, which suits 'musical'; split it into two toms, male felines.
explanation.definitionFit: Andrew Lloyd Webber's show based on T. S. Eliot's poems, and toms are male felines.

clue.text: Aim to express disapproval

blocks.note: first meaning: a goal or purpose, as a noun
second meaning: to protest, as a verb

explanation.surface: Setting out with the purpose of complaining.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun means a goal or purpose; the verb means to raise a protest against something.

clue.text: Succeeded with anything attempted

blocks.note: s. is the genealogical abbreviation for succeeded
ought, a variant of aught, means anything

explanation.surface: Someone managed whatever they tried their hand at.
explanation.walkthrough: Ought is an old spelling of aught, meaning anything at all.
explanation.definitionFit: To have sought to do something is to have tried or endeavoured to do it.

clue.text: Made fun of conductor in audition

indicators.note: an audition is a hearing, so the word is taken by how it sounds

blocks.note: a guide conducts people around

explanation.surface: Orchestra players mocked the conductor at a tryout.
explanation.walkthrough: The conductor leads tourists, not an orchestra, and audition means hearing, not a tryout.
explanation.definitionFit: To guy someone is to ridicule them, from the effigies of Guy Fawkes.

clue.text: Vehicle turned and set out to be of assistance

indicators.note: a turned vehicle faces the other way, so the word is read backwards

blocks.note: a bus is a road vehicle
to serve food is to set it out

explanation.surface: A van performs a U-turn and departs to help someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set out' suggests departing, but it means laying out, as a meal is served.
explanation.definitionFit: To subserve is to promote or further a purpose, serving it as a means.

clue.text: Failing to catch all-rounder, say

indicators.note: to catch something is to hold it, so one piece holds the other

blocks.note: a vice is a moral failing
O is a letter that is round all over

explanation.surface: A cricket fielder drops a catch off an all-rounder.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, an all-rounder both bats and bowls; here it is just the round letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: To voice an opinion is to say it, express it in words.

clue.text: Bad-tempered, as a seal may be

blocks.note: first meaning: British slang for angry, from 'in a wax'
second meaning: made of the material used to seal letters

explanation.surface: A grumpy creature, like a seal can be.
explanation.walkthrough: The seal is the stamp pressed into hot wax, not the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: Old British slang 'in a wax' means in a rage, and sealing material for letters is traditionally wax.

clue.text: Place in university for bookish types

definitions.note: plural people for a collective noun

blocks.note: first meaning: the post of a reader, a senior lecturer in British universities
second meaning: the body of people who read a publication

explanation.surface: A university position suited to studious people.
explanation.walkthrough: In British universities a reader ranks just below a professor.
explanation.definitionFit: The academic rank of a reader, and also the collective audience of a newspaper or magazine.

clue.text: Paid footballer for informative response

blocks.note: read as fee'd, given a fee
a back is a defensive player

explanation.surface: A professional footballer gives a useful reply to a question.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Paid' is read as fee'd, that is, given a fee.
explanation.definitionFit: Feedback is comment on performance that tells someone how they are doing.

clue.text: Person going round the bend's an artist

blocks.note: first meaning: one who turns a corner
second meaning: J. M. W. ..., the English painter

explanation.surface: An artist is someone who is going mad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going round the bend' suggests madness, but it is just turning a corner.
explanation.definitionFit: One who turns is literally a turner, and J. M. W. Turner was the English Romantic landscape painter.
